question: What is the main difference between artificial and natural immunity?

options.A: It lasts for only a few days in the body
options.B: It is acquired through deliberate medical intervention
options.C: It is passed directly from mother to child
options.D: It only protects against bacterial infections

explanation: Artificial immunity requires a medical action like an injection, whereas natural immunity happens through daily life exposure or pregnancy. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h1)

question: How is artificial immunity typically gained?

options.A: Inhaling dust particles containing active viruses in a market
options.B: Receiving medical products like vaccines or immune globulins
options.C: Breastfeeding an infant during the first six months of life
options.D: Contracting the wild disease and recovering from it naturally

explanation: Medical products such as vaccines and immune globulins are specifically designed to create or provide artificial protection. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h1)

question: What is the primary substance introduced into the body during active artificial immunization?

options.A: Strong chemical antibiotics that kill all bacteria instantly
options.B: A modified or weakened form of a disease-causing antigen
options.C: Pure white blood cells taken from a healthy adult
options.D: Ready-made antibodies collected from a human donor

explanation: Vaccines contain harmless or weakened parts of germs so the immune system learns to fight them without getting sick. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h2)

question: Why does active artificial immunity take time to provide full protection after a vaccine is given?

options.A: The body needs time to manufacture its own memory cells and antibodies
options.B: White blood cells must migrate slowly from the bone marrow to the skin
options.C: The injected medicine must circulate through the blood for weeks to dissolve
options.D: The vaccine virus must slowly multiply until it fills the whole body

explanation: Active immunity requires your own cells to do the work of building antibodies and memory cells, which takes several days to weeks. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h2)

question: What is the main characteristic of passive artificial immunity?

options.A: It stimulates the bone marrow to produce lasting memory cells
options.B: It requires several booster doses over a period of many years
options.C: It takes at least one month before any antibodies appear
options.D: It provides immediate protection using ready-made antibodies

explanation: Passive immunity gives you ready-made antibodies right away so you do not have to wait for your body to make them. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h3)

question: Which scenario best calls for the use of passive artificial immunity rather than a vaccine?

options.A: A school-aged child getting a measles booster before entering primary school
options.B: A healthy newborn baby receiving the routine birth dose of the BCG vaccine
options.C: A patient with a deep, dirty puncture wound who might have contracted tetanus
options.D: A pregnant woman attending a routine antenatal clinic for malaria prevention

explanation: When an infection or toxin can act faster than a vaccine can stimulate the body, ready-made antibodies (antitoxin) are needed urgently. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h3)

question: Which cells are responsible for remembering a vaccine antigen for a long time?
explanation: Memory lymphocytes stay in the body for a long time to recognize the germ immediately if it attacks later. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h4)

question: What happens when memory cells encounter the real disease germ months after vaccination?

options.A: They cause a severe allergic reaction because they confuse the germ
options.B: They trigger a fast and powerful immune response before illness develops
options.C: They wait for macrophages to come and teach them what the germ looks like
options.D: They destroy all the normal white blood cells to make room for new ones

explanation: Memory cells remember the training from the vaccine, allowing the body to react so quickly that the disease cannot take over. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h4)

question: How long does protection typically last with active artificial immunity?
explanation: Active immunity creates memory cells that protect the body for many years or even for life. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h5)

question: A woman accidentally steps on a rusty nail at a farm and has not had a tetanus shot in ten years. Which type of artificial protection does she need right away?

options.A: No medical treatment is needed since rusty nails only cause minor skin irritation
options.B: Oral antibiotics only, because bacteria cannot survive in deep muscle tissue
options.C: Passive immunity through tetanus antitoxin or immunoglobulin for immediate defense
options.D: Active immunity through a tetanus vaccine so she can build her own antibodies next month

explanation: Tetanus is fast-acting and dangerous, so a patient with a dirty wound needs immediate ready-made antibodies rather than waiting weeks for a vaccine to work. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h5)

question: Why is tetanus toxoid vaccine given to pregnant women during antenatal care in Nigeria?

options.A: To stop excessive bleeding during the third stage of labor
options.B: To cure active malaria infections in the placenta
options.C: To increase the total volume of amniotic fluid
options.D: To prevent neonatal tetanus in the newborn baby

explanation: Pregnant women receive tetanus toxoid so they can pass protective antibodies to the baby, preventing fatal neonatal tetanus. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h6)

question: A Rhesus-negative mother gives birth to a Rhesus-positive baby at a primary health centre. What clinical action should the midwife take to protect future pregnancies?

options.A: Inject the newborn baby with strong bacterial antibiotics immediately
options.B: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin to provide passive artificial protection
options.C: Advise the mother that no medical intervention is ever necessary
options.D: Give the mother a live oral polio vaccine to stimulate active immunity

explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin destroys any fetal red blood cells that entered the mother's circulation, preventing her body from forming antibodies that could harm future Rhesus-positive babies. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T10#BMP111_U6_T10_h6)
